name: Kurose 1950s survey
notes: Every linear dimension is in GROUND METRES and carries an 'M' suffix; the
loader rejects unit-less numbers in dimension sections. See
tools/city-map/citymap/style.py for why -- pixel dimensions make previews
Values marked 'was Npx' were literal pixels in the original spike, tuned at
0.586 m/px (the 12 km frame at 20480px working canvas). They have been
converted at that scale so the delivered render is unchanged, and now scale

pageFurniture._note: Page-relative, NOT ground metres -- these are properties of the sheet (see style.py). Fractions of the page's output width unless suffixed Px.

buildingMaterial._note: building:material -> flat fill colour, overriding the generic height-graded buildingLow/buildingHigh lerp above for a building tagged this way -- set by the Scratchpad's Fill tool (editor/static/scratchpad.js's MATERIAL_STYLES) or by hand. Still gets shadow_mul-multiplied like any other building fill, so it darkens correctly in cast shadow.

canopy._note: Vegetation-canopy noise tint for forest/wood/scrub landuse (citymap.render.CANOPY_LANDUSE_KEYS), replacing their flat landuse colour above -- added 2026-08-24 after a direct user report of blocky/low-res-looking forest fill next to crisp contour lines (real cause: coarse OSM forest polygon data, made worse by a single flat tint with no internal variation). Palette stops loosely sampled from a real aerial photo of autumn forest near Kobe: darker sage, the existing forest/wood tone, olive/amber, and a sparse warm rust accent -- gamma biases the noise toward the first two stops so the mountains don't shift the whole map's colour temperature, only read as textured.

lighting._coastFadeNote: Direct user request 2026-08-24: bare (unclassified) terrain reads as a warm brown right up to the coast -- paper tinted by warmTint at whatever brightness that patch of ground happens to have, no landuse tint to soften it (an already-tagged landuse like sand/aerodrome keeps its own colour untouched, this only affects untagged ground). A wide fade toward palette.coastFade near the shoreline reads as an intentional coastal fringe instead of an abrupt or jagged boundary -- see fields.coast_fade_t and render_tile's own coastal-fade section. coastFadeM is deliberately large ('very large wide fade', the user's own words), much bigger than sea's own falloff.
